# Support vector machines {#sec-ch-mla-svm}

> *"The support-vector network is a new learning machine for two-group
> classification problems."* — Corinna Cortes and Vladimir Vapnik, 1995
> [@cortes1995]

```{python}
#| echo: false
import mlalgbook
mlalgbook.setup()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- **prove** the formula for the distance of a point from a hyperplane and
  derive the **maximal margin classifier** as a convex quadratic problem with
  a unique solution;
- extend it to the **soft margin** with slack variables, **prove** that this
  is regularised empirical risk minimisation with the **hinge loss**, and
  explain the role of $C$ and the influence of outliers;
- derive the **dual problem** and the **KKT conditions**, explain why only the
  **support vectors** matter, and **prove** the leave-one-out bound
  "error ≤ fraction of support vectors";
- use **kernels** — linear, polynomial, RBF, sigmoid — **prove** that a
  kernel defined by a feature map has positive semidefinite Gram matrices and
  that the RBF kernel corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature map;
- train and tune SVMs in scikit-learn (`SVC`, `LinearSVC`), with scaling, $C$
  and $\gamma$ chosen by cross-validation, for two or more classes.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## Topics covered
The support vector classifier; non-linear relationships; kernels and the
kernel trick; in practice, the maximal margin classifier, soft margins, linear
SVMs, the effect of outliers, and SVMs with linear, polynomial, sigmoid and
Gaussian (RBF) kernels.
:::

## Intuition: the widest street {#sec-svm-intuition}

Two groups of points on a plane can be separated by many straight lines.
Logistic regression picks the line that makes the observed labels most
probable; a support vector machine picks the line that leaves the **widest
empty street** between the two groups, with the line down the middle of it.
The idea is that a boundary far from all training points is robust: small
perturbations of the points, or new points similar to them, stay on the
correct side.

Two consequences make the method distinctive. First, the street is determined
only by the points on its edges — the **support vectors**; all the others
could move (without crossing the edges) or disappear without changing
anything. Second, the computation depends on the data only through **inner
products** between points; replacing them by a **kernel** lets the same
algorithm draw curved boundaries, as if the points had been mapped into a
space with many more dimensions, without ever computing that map.

## The maximal margin classifier {#sec-svm-max-margin}

A **hyperplane** in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is the set $\{x : w^\top x + b = 0\}$ with
$w \neq 0$; the **linear classifier** it defines predicts $\operatorname{sign}
(w^\top x + b)$. In this chapter the labels are $y_i \in \{-1, +1\}$, so that
"$x_i$ is on the correct side" reads $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) > 0$.

::: {#prp-svm-distance}
## Distance from a hyperplane
The (Euclidean) distance of a point $x_0$ from the hyperplane $w^\top x + b = 0$
is $|w^\top x_0 + b|/\lVert w\rVert$, and $(w^\top x_0 + b)/\lVert w\rVert$ is
the **signed distance**, positive on the side towards which $w$ points.
:::

*In one line:* the score $w^\top x + b$ is the distance from the boundary
measured in units of $1/\lVert w\rVert$.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-svm-distance
$w$ is orthogonal to the hyperplane: for two points $x, x'$ on it, $w^\top(x -
x') = 0$. The closest point of the hyperplane to $x_0$ is therefore $x_0 - tw$
for the $t$ that puts it on the hyperplane: $w^\top(x_0 - tw) + b = 0$ gives
$t = (w^\top x_0 + b)/\lVert w\rVert^2$, and the distance is $\lVert
tw\rVert = |w^\top x_0 + b|/\lVert w\rVert$. (Any other point $x$ of the
hyperplane is farther: $\lVert x_0 - x\rVert^2 = \lVert tw\rVert^2 + \lVert
x_0 - tw - x\rVert^2$ by Pythagoras, as $x_0 - tw - x$ lies in the hyperplane's
direction, orthogonal to $w$.) $\blacksquare$
:::

The **margin** of a separating hyperplane is the distance from it to the
closest training point, $\min_iy_i(w^\top x_i + b)/\lVert w\rVert$. Scaling
$(w, b)$ by any $c > 0$ changes neither the hyperplane nor the margin, so we
may fix the scale by requiring that the closest points have $y_i(w^\top x_i +
b) = 1$: the margin is then $1/\lVert w\rVert$, and maximising it means
minimising $\lVert w\rVert$.

::: {#thm-svm-hard-margin}
## The maximal margin classifier
If the two classes are linearly separable, the hyperplane with the largest
margin is given by the solution of
$$
\min_{w, b}\;\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2
\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1,\quad i = 1, \dots, n,
$$ {#eq-svm-hard}
its margin is $1/\lVert w^*\rVert$, and the solution $(w^*, b^*)$ is unique.
:::

*In one line:* the widest street is the solution of a convex problem — a
quadratic objective with linear constraints — and there is exactly one.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-svm-hard-margin
Equivalence: any separating $(w, b)$ can be rescaled so that $\min_iy_i(w^\top
x_i + b) = 1$; it is then feasible for @eq-svm-hard with margin $1/\lVert
w\rVert$. Conversely, a feasible $(w, b)$ separates with margin at least
$1/\lVert w\rVert$, and at the optimum some constraint is active (otherwise
$(w, b)$ could be scaled down, decreasing $\lVert w\rVert$), so the margin is
exactly $1/\lVert w^*\rVert$. Maximising the margin is minimising $\lVert
w\rVert$. Existence: the feasible set is closed and non-empty, and the
objective grows without bound in $w$; for fixed $w \neq 0$ the feasible $b$
form a closed bounded interval (both classes are present), so a minimum
exists. Uniqueness of $w$: if $w_1 \neq w_2$ were both optimal with value $m$,
their midpoint (with the midpoint of the $b$'s) is feasible, the constraints
being linear, and $\lVert\frac{w_1 + w_2}{2}\rVert^2 < \frac12\lVert
w_1\rVert^2 + \frac12\lVert w_2\rVert^2 = 2m$ by strict convexity of the
squared norm — a contradiction. Uniqueness of $b$: with $w^*$ fixed, $b$ must
satisfy $b \ge 1 - w^{*\top}x_i$ for the positive and $b \le -1 -
w^{*\top}x_i$ for the negative points; if the interval of feasible $b$ had
positive length, $w^*$ could be shrunk slightly with some $b$ still feasible,
contradicting optimality. $\blacksquare$
:::

::: {#exm-svm-hand}
## The widest street by hand
With one point per class, $x_+ = (3, 3)$ and $x_- = (1, 1)$, the widest street
is the perpendicular bisector of the segment between them. Both constraints
are active: $w^\top x_+ + b = 1$, $w^\top x_- + b = -1$, and $w$ is parallel to
$x_+ - x_- = (2, 2)$, say $w = (a, a)$. Subtracting, $w^\top(x_+ - x_-) = 4a =
2$, so $w = (0.5, 0.5)$, and $b = 1 - 0.5\cdot3 - 0.5\cdot3 = -2$. The
boundary is $x_1 + x_2 = 4$, through the midpoint $(2, 2)$; the margin is
$1/\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt2$, half the distance between the points.
:::

```{python}
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.svm import SVC, LinearSVC

hand = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit([[3, 3], [1, 1]], [1, -1])      # huge C: effectively a hard margin
print("w =", hand.coef_[0].round(4), " b =", hand.intercept_.round(4), " margin =", round(1 / np.linalg.norm(hand.coef_), 4))
```

`SVC` solves the soft-margin problem of the next section; with a very large
$C$ it coincides with the hard margin on separable data.

```{python}
#| label: fig-svm-hard-margin
#| fig-cap: "Maximal margin classifier on 40 separable points. The solid line is the boundary, the dashed lines the edges of the street (score ±1); circled points are the support vectors — the only points that determine the solution."
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
Xs = np.vstack([rng.normal([2, 2], 0.6, (20, 2)), rng.normal([-1, -0.5], 0.6, (20, 2))])
ys = np.repeat([1, -1], 20)
hard = SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit(Xs, ys)

def draw_svm(ax, model, X, y, title=""):
    """Points, boundary, street edges and support vectors of a fitted linear SVC."""
    w, b = model.coef_[0], model.intercept_[0]
    xs = np.linspace(X[:, 0].min() - 1, X[:, 0].max() + 1, 2)
    for level, style in ((0, "-"), (1, "--"), (-1, "--")):
        ax.plot(xs, (level - b - w[0] * xs) / w[1], color=mlalgbook.INK2, ls=style, lw=1.2)
    for k, c in zip((-1, 1), mlalgbook.COLORS):
        ax.scatter(*X[y == k].T, s=22, color=c, edgecolor="#fcfcfb", linewidth=0.5, label=f"y = {k:+d}", zorder=3)
    sv = model.support_vectors_
    ax.scatter(*sv.T, s=110, facecolor="none", edgecolor=mlalgbook.INK, linewidth=1, zorder=4)
    ax.set_ylim(X[:, 1].min() - 1, X[:, 1].max() + 1); ax.set_title(title); ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="datalim")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4))
draw_svm(ax, hard, Xs, ys); ax.legend(loc="upper left"); plt.show()
print(f"{len(hard.support_)} support vectors out of {len(ys)}; margin = {1 / np.linalg.norm(hard.coef_):.3f}")
```

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla4-margin-easy}
## Easy — distances and margin
For the hyperplane $2x_1 - x_2 + 1 = 0$, compute the signed distances of
$(1, 1)$, $(0, 3)$ and $(-1, -1)$. If the labels are $+1, -1, +1$, is the
hyperplane separating, and what is its margin?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$\lVert w\rVert = \sqrt5$. The point is on the correct side when
$y_i(w^\top x_i + b) > 0$; the margin is the smallest $y_i(w^\top x_i +
b)/\lVert w\rVert$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Scores: $2 - 1 + 1 = 2$, $0 - 3 + 1 = -2$, $-2 + 1 + 1 = 0$. Signed distances
$2/\sqrt5 \approx 0.894$, $-0.894$, $0$. The third point lies **on** the
hyperplane: $y_3\cdot0 = 0$ is not $> 0$, so the hyperplane does not separate
the data strictly, and its margin is $0$.
```{python}
w0, b0 = np.array([2, -1]), 1
P3, y3 = np.array([[1, 1], [0, 3], [-1, -1]]), np.array([1, -1, 1])
print("signed distances:", ((P3 @ w0 + b0) / np.linalg.norm(w0)).round(3), " margin:", (y3 * (P3 @ w0 + b0) / np.linalg.norm(w0)).min())
```
A frequent slip is to forget the division by $\lVert w\rVert$: the raw scores
$\pm2$ are not distances, and they change if the equation is multiplied by a
constant.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-margin-medium}
## Medium — the hard-margin problem with a generic solver
Solve @eq-svm-hard for the 40 points of @fig-svm-hard-margin with
`scipy.optimize.minimize` (method `"SLSQP"`, the constraints as inequality
constraints), and compare $w$, $b$ and the margin with `SVC(kernel="linear",
C=1e6)`. Which constraints are active at the solution?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Optimise over $\theta = (w_1, w_2, b)$; the constraint function returns the
vector $y_i(w^\top x_i + b) - 1$, which must be $\ge 0$. Active constraints
are those with value (numerically) zero.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from scipy.optimize import minimize
cons = {"type": "ineq", "fun": lambda t: ys * (Xs @ t[:2] + t[2]) - 1, "jac": lambda t: ys[:, None] * np.column_stack([Xs, np.ones(len(ys))])}
res = minimize(lambda t: 0.5 * t[:2] @ t[:2], x0=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 0.0]), jac=lambda t: np.array([t[0], t[1], 0.0]),
               constraints=[cons], method="SLSQP", options={"ftol": 1e-12, "maxiter": 500})
active = np.where(np.abs(ys * (Xs @ res.x[:2] + res.x[2]) - 1) < 1e-6)[0]
print("SLSQP:  w =", res.x[:2].round(4), "b =", round(res.x[2], 4), "margin", round(1 / np.linalg.norm(res.x[:2]), 4))
print("SVC:    w =", hard.coef_[0].round(4), "b =", hard.intercept_.round(4)[0], "| active constraints:", active, "| SVC support:", np.sort(hard.support_))
```
The generic solver and `SVC` agree, and the active constraints are exactly
the support vectors. A general-purpose solver is fine for 40 points; SVM
libraries use specialised algorithms (SMO, @sec-svm-dual) because the number
of constraints equals the number of examples. A common mistake is to start
the solver at an infeasible point and not check `res.success`.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-margin-hard}
## Hard — one point can move the street
Add to the 40 points of @fig-svm-hard-margin a single new point with label
$+1$ placed close to the negative group — e.g. at $(0.3, 0.6)$ — so that the
data remain separable. Fit the hard-margin SVM again, and also soft-margin
SVMs with $C = 1$ and $C = 0.1$. Plot the four solutions and report the
margins and the number of support vectors. What does this suggest about
detecting and handling outliers before training?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Reuse `draw_svm` on a $2 \times 2$ grid of axes. Check separability by
verifying that the hard-margin solution classifies all training points
correctly.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| label: fig-svm-outlier
#| fig-cap: "A single point (+1, near the other class) and four SVMs. The hard margin (top right) bends the whole boundary to accommodate it; soft margins with smaller C let it violate the street and keep a boundary close to the original."
X_out, y_out = np.vstack([Xs, [[0.3, 0.6]]]), np.append(ys, 1)
fits = [("original data, hard margin", SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit(Xs, ys), Xs, ys),
        ("with the new point, hard margin", SVC(kernel="linear", C=1e6).fit(X_out, y_out), X_out, y_out),
        ("with the new point, C = 1", SVC(kernel="linear", C=1).fit(X_out, y_out), X_out, y_out),
        ("with the new point, C = 0.1", SVC(kernel="linear", C=0.1).fit(X_out, y_out), X_out, y_out)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(9, 7.5))
for ax, (title, m, X_, y_) in zip(axes.ravel(), fits):
    draw_svm(ax, m, X_, y_, title)
    print(f"{title:32s}: margin {1 / np.linalg.norm(m.coef_):.3f}, support vectors {len(m.support_)}, training accuracy {m.score(X_, y_):.3f}")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
The hard margin must keep every point outside the street, so one unusual
point narrows the margin dramatically and tilts the boundary. With a finite
$C$ the point is allowed inside the street (or on the wrong side) at a cost,
and the boundary stays close to the original one, with a wider margin and more
support vectors. Removing a point is a decision about the *data* (is it an
error of measurement or labelling?), while lowering $C$ is a decision about
the *model*; the first should be justified by inspecting the point, never by
the fact that it hurts the fit. The typical mistake is to delete inconvenient
points to improve the score.
:::

## Soft margins and the hinge loss {#sec-svm-soft-margin}

Real classes overlap, and @eq-svm-hard then has no solution. The **soft
margin** of Cortes and Vapnik [@cortes1995] allows each point a **slack**
$\xi_i \ge 0$ — how far it is on the wrong side of its edge of the street —
at a price $C$ per unit:
$$
\min_{w, b, \xi}\;\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_i
\quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(w^\top x_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i,\;\; \xi_i \ge 0 .
$$ {#eq-svm-soft}
A point with $0 < \xi_i \le 1$ is inside the street but correctly classified;
with $\xi_i > 1$ it is misclassified. The constrained form hides a familiar
structure.

::: {#thm-svm-hinge}
## The soft margin is regularised hinge-loss minimisation
@eq-svm-soft is equivalent to the unconstrained problem
$$
\min_{w, b}\;\sum_{i=1}^n\max\big(0,\,1 - y_i(w^\top x_i + b)\big) + \frac{1}{2C}\lVert w\rVert^2 ,
$$ {#eq-svm-hinge}
that is, empirical risk minimisation with the **hinge loss** $\ell(y, f) =
\max(0, 1 - yf)$ and an L2 penalty of strength $\lambda = 1/C$. The hinge loss
is convex and is an upper bound on the 0–1 loss: $\max(0, 1 - yf) \ge
\mathbb{1}\{yf \le 0\}$.
:::

*In one line:* an SVM is a penalised linear model like ridge or logistic
regression — only the loss is different, and $C$ is the inverse of the
penalty: large $C$, weak regularisation.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-svm-hinge
For fixed $(w, b)$, @eq-svm-soft minimises $\sum_i\xi_i$ subject to $\xi_i \ge
1 - y_i(w^\top x_i + b)$ and $\xi_i \ge 0$; the smallest feasible value is
$\xi_i = \max(0, 1 - y_i(w^\top x_i + b))$. Substituting it, the problem in
$(w, b)$ is $\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\max(0, 1 - y_if_i)$; dividing by
$C > 0$ does not change the minimiser. The hinge is the maximum of two affine
functions of $f$, hence convex; and if $yf \le 0$ then $1 - yf \ge 1$, while
it is always $\ge 0$. $\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-svm-losses
#| fig-cap: "Losses as functions of the margin yf: the 0–1 loss, the hinge loss of the SVM, and the logistic loss of logistic regression (in base 2, so that it equals 1 at yf = 0). Both convex losses bound the 0–1 loss from above; the hinge is exactly zero beyond yf = 1 — points well inside their side have no influence at all."
m = np.linspace(-2.5, 3, 500)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.plot(m, (m <= 0).astype(float), label="0–1 loss", color=mlalgbook.MUTED)
ax.plot(m, np.maximum(0, 1 - m), label="hinge (SVM)")
ax.plot(m, np.log2(1 + np.exp(-m)), label="logistic, base 2")
ax.set_xlabel("margin y·f(x)"); ax.set_ylabel("loss"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
```

The flat part of the hinge is the source of the support vectors: a point with
$y_if_i > 1$ contributes nothing to the objective, so it does not influence
the solution; with the logistic loss every point pulls a little. The
parameter $C$ trades the width of the street against the violations: small
$C$ means a strong penalty on $\lVert w\rVert$, a wide street, many points
inside it (many support vectors) and a smoother, more biased boundary; large
$C$ a narrow street that tries to classify every training point.

```{python}
#| echo: false
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
_r = np.random.default_rng(11)
_X = np.vstack([_r.normal([1.2, 1.0], 1.0, (40, 2)), _r.normal([-1.0, -0.8], 1.0, (40, 2))])
_y = np.repeat([1, -1], 40)
_Cs = np.logspace(-3, 2, 21)
_fits = []
for _C in _Cs:
    _m = SVC(kernel="linear", C=_C).fit(_X, _y)
    _fits.append({"C": float(_C), "w": _m.coef_[0].tolist(), "b": float(_m.intercept_[0]),
                  "sv": _m.support_.tolist(), "train": float(_m.score(_X, _y)),
                  "cv": float(cross_val_score(SVC(kernel="linear", C=_C), _X, _y, cv=5).mean())})
ojs_define(svmPts=[{"x": float(a), "y": float(b), "label": int(c)} for (a, b), c in zip(_X, _y)], svmFits=_fits)
```

::: {.widget}
```{ojs}

```

svmLines = {
  const [w0, w1] = svmFit.w, b = svmFit.b, out = [];
  for (const [level, kind] of [[0, "boundary"], [1, "edge +1"], [-1, "edge −1"]])
    for (const x of [-4.5, 4.5]) out.push({x, y: (level - b - w0 * x) / w1, kind});

  color: {type: "ordinal", domain: [-1, 1], range: ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834"], legend: true},

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla4-soft-easy}
## Easy — slacks and hinge losses
For $w = (1, 0)$, $b = 0$ and the points $(2, 0)$ with $y = +1$, $(0.5, 1)$
with $y = +1$, $(-0.2, 0)$ with $y = +1$ and $(0.3, 0)$ with $y = -1$,
compute the margins $y_if_i$, the slacks, the hinge losses, and which points
are correctly classified, inside the street, or misclassified. Evaluate
@eq-svm-hinge for $C = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$f(x) = x_1$. Slack $= \max(0, 1 - yf)$; inside the street means $0 < yf <
1$, misclassified $yf < 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$yf = 2, 0.5, -0.2, -0.3$; slacks $0, 0.5, 1.2, 1.3$. Point 1 is outside the
street (no loss), point 2 inside the street but correct, points 3 and 4
misclassified. Objective: $3.0 + \frac12\cdot1 = 3.5$.
```{python}
Pq, yq, wq = np.array([[2, 0], [0.5, 1], [-0.2, 0], [0.3, 0]]), np.array([1, 1, 1, -1]), np.array([1.0, 0.0])
marg = yq * (Pq @ wq); hinge = np.maximum(0, 1 - marg)
print("margins", marg, "hinge", hinge, "objective", hinge.sum() + 0.5 * wq @ wq)
```
Point 2 is correctly classified yet pays a loss: the hinge penalises being
correct *without enough margin*. That is what makes the street, and what a
common reading ("the SVM only cares about mistakes") misses.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-soft-medium}
## Medium — a linear SVM by stochastic subgradient descent
Implement the **Pegasos** algorithm [@shalevshwartz2011] for @eq-svm-hinge
without intercept (append a constant feature instead): at step $t$ pick a
random example, set $\eta_t = 1/(\lambda t)$, and update $w \leftarrow (1 -
\eta_t\lambda)w + \eta_ty_ix_i$ if $y_iw^\top x_i < 1$, else $w \leftarrow
(1 - \eta_t\lambda)w$, where the objective is $\frac\lambda2\lVert w\rVert^2 +
\frac1n\sum_i\text{hinge}_i$. Run it on the standardised breast-cancer data
and compare objective value and accuracy with `LinearSVC` at the matching $C$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Multiplying @eq-svm-hinge by $C/n$ gives $\frac1n\sum\text{hinge} +
\frac{1}{2Cn}\lVert w\rVert^2$, so $\lambda = 1/(Cn)$. `LinearSVC(loss="hinge",
fit_intercept=False)` solves exactly @eq-svm-hinge without intercept. Compare
the objective values, which are a fairer test than the coefficients.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xb, yb01 = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
Xb1 = np.column_stack([StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xb), np.ones(len(yb01))])   # constant feature in place of b
yb = 2 * yb01 - 1
n_b, C = len(yb), 1.0
lam = 1 / (C * n_b)
objective = lambda w: lam / 2 * w @ w + np.mean(np.maximum(0, 1 - yb * (Xb1 @ w)))
rp, w = np.random.default_rng(0), np.zeros(Xb1.shape[1])
for t in range(1, 200_001):
    i = rp.integers(n_b); eta = 1 / (lam * t)
    if yb[i] * (Xb1[i] @ w) < 1:
        w = (1 - eta * lam) * w + eta * yb[i] * Xb1[i]
    else:
        w = (1 - eta * lam) * w
lsvc = LinearSVC(C=C, loss="hinge", fit_intercept=False, max_iter=200_000, tol=1e-8).fit(Xb1, yb)
print(f"Pegasos:   objective {objective(w):.5f}, training accuracy {np.mean(np.sign(Xb1 @ w) == yb):.4f}")
print(f"LinearSVC: objective {objective(lsvc.coef_[0]):.5f}, training accuracy {lsvc.score(Xb1, yb):.4f}")
```
After 200 000 cheap steps Pegasos is within a small fraction of the optimal
objective. Its step $1/(\lambda t)$ is the strongly convex schedule of
@sec-opt-schedules; with $\lambda = 1/(Cn)$ tiny, the first steps are huge,
which is why many iterations are needed. Note that the constant feature is
penalised along with $w$, unlike a true intercept; `LinearSVC` with
`fit_intercept=True` also penalises its intercept (it is implemented the same
way), unlike `SVC` — a detail that matters only with poorly centred data.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-soft-hard}
## Hard — choosing $C$ for three classes
On the wine data, tune $C$ for `LinearSVC` (inside a pipeline with
`StandardScaler`) by 5-fold cross-validation over a logarithmic grid; estimate
the accuracy of the whole procedure by nested cross-validation; and compare
the confusion matrices of `LinearSVC` (one-vs-rest) and `SVC(kernel="linear")`
(one-vs-one) on a held-out test split. Which classes are confused, and does
the multi-class strategy matter here?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`GridSearchCV` inside `cross_val_score` gives the nested estimate (@sec-selection).
Fit both final models on the same training split. With three classes,
one-vs-rest trains 3 classifiers and one-vs-one 3 as well — but different ones.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, StratifiedKFold, train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix

Xw, yw = load_wine(return_X_y=True)
grid = {"linearsvc__C": np.logspace(-3, 2, 11)}
inner, outer = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0), StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)
search = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearSVC(max_iter=20_000)), grid, cv=inner)
nested = cross_val_score(search, Xw, yw, cv=outer)
print(f"nested CV accuracy {nested.mean():.3f} ± {nested.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(5):.3f}")
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xw, yw, test_size=0.3, stratify=yw, random_state=0)
ovr = search.fit(Xtr, ytr)
ovo = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear")), {"svc__C": np.logspace(-3, 2, 11)}, cv=inner).fit(Xtr, ytr)
for name, mdl in (("LinearSVC, one-vs-rest", ovr), ("SVC linear, one-vs-one", ovo)):
    print(f"{name}: best C {list(mdl.best_params_.values())[0]:.3g}, test accuracy {mdl.score(Xte, yte):.3f}")
    print(confusion_matrix(yte, mdl.predict(Xte)))
```
The wine classes are almost linearly separable after standardisation, so both
strategies reach very high accuracy and the confusion matrices differ by at
most a wine or two; the nested estimate, not the test split alone, is the
number to report. With many classes the strategies differ more: one-vs-one
trains $K(K-1)/2$ small problems, one-vs-rest $K$ large and unbalanced ones.
Typical mistakes: reporting the best inner CV score as the accuracy, and
forgetting the scaler (an SVM's margin is measured in the units of the
features, so a feature with a large range dominates it).
:::

## Duality, KKT conditions and support vectors {#sec-svm-dual}

The constrained problem @eq-svm-soft has a **dual** that is the key to both
efficient algorithms and kernels. Introduce a multiplier $\alpha_i \ge 0$ for
each margin constraint and $\mu_i \ge 0$ for each $\xi_i \ge 0$; the
**Lagrangian** is
$$
\mathcal{L} = \frac12\lVert w\rVert^2 + C\sum_i\xi_i - \sum_i\alpha_i\big(y_i(w^\top x_i + b) - 1 + \xi_i\big) - \sum_i\mu_i\xi_i .
$$

::: {#thm-svm-dual}
## The dual problem and the support vectors
The dual of @eq-svm-soft is
$$
\max_\alpha\;\sum_i\alpha_i - \frac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_jy_iy_j\,x_i^\top x_j
\quad\text{subject to}\quad 0 \le \alpha_i \le C,\;\; \sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0,
$$ {#eq-svm-dual}
the optimal values of the two problems are equal, and the solutions are linked
by
$$
w^* = \sum_i\alpha_i^*y_ix_i .
$$ {#eq-svm-w}
Moreover (**complementary slackness**): if $y_if(x_i) > 1$ then $\alpha_i^* =
0$; if $0 < \alpha_i^* < C$ then $y_if(x_i) = 1$ (the point is on an edge of
the street); and if $y_if(x_i) < 1$ then $\alpha_i^* = C$.
:::

*In one line:* the solution is a weighted sum of training points, and only the
points on or inside the street — the **support vectors** — have non-zero
weight; every other point could be deleted without changing the classifier.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-svm-dual
**Dual function.** For fixed multipliers, minimise $\mathcal{L}$ over the
primal variables. $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial w = w - \sum_i\alpha_iy_ix_i =
0$ gives @eq-svm-w; $\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial b = -\sum_i\alpha_iy_i$ must
vanish, otherwise $\mathcal{L}$ is unbounded below in $b$; $\partial
\mathcal{L}/\partial\xi_i = C - \alpha_i - \mu_i = 0$, otherwise unbounded in
$\xi_i$. Substituting, the $\xi$ and $b$ terms vanish and $\frac12\lVert
w\rVert^2 - \sum_i\alpha_iy_iw^\top x_i = -\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2$, giving the
objective of @eq-svm-dual; $\mu_i = C - \alpha_i \ge 0$ gives $\alpha_i \le C$.
**Weak duality**: for any primal-feasible point and $\alpha, \mu \ge 0$, the
subtracted terms of $\mathcal{L}$ are non-negative, so $\mathcal{L} \le$
primal objective, and the dual function (a minimum of $\mathcal{L}$) is at
most the primal objective at every feasible point. **Strong duality**: the
primal is a convex quadratic problem with affine constraints and is feasible
(take $w = 0$, $b = 0$, $\xi_i = 1$), so the duality gap is zero and both
optima are attained [@boyd2004, §5.2.3 and §5.5.3]. At the optimum, then, the
**KKT conditions** hold, among them $\alpha_i(y_if_i - 1 + \xi_i) = 0$ and
$\mu_i\xi_i = (C - \alpha_i)\xi_i = 0$. If $y_if_i > 1$ then $\xi_i = 0$ and
$y_if_i - 1 + \xi_i > 0$, so $\alpha_i = 0$. If $0 < \alpha_i < C$, the second
condition gives $\xi_i = 0$ and the first $y_if_i = 1$. If $y_if_i < 1$, then
$\xi_i \ge 1 - y_if_i > 0$, so $\alpha_i = C$. $\blacksquare$
:::

The intercept follows from any **free** support vector ($0 < \alpha_i < C$),
for which $y_i(w^{*\top}x_i + b) = 1$, i.e. $b = y_i - w^{*\top}x_i$
(libraries average over all free support vectors). The dual is what libsvm,
the solver behind `SVC`, actually solves, with Platt's **sequential minimal
optimisation** (SMO): it repeatedly picks two multipliers and optimises over
them analytically, the smallest step that respects $\sum_i\alpha_iy_i = 0$
[@platt1998; @chang2011].

Sparsity has a statistical consequence.

::: {#thm-svm-loo}
## The leave-one-out bound
For the maximal margin classifier (and for any problem where the solution
does not change when a non-support vector is removed), the leave-one-out
cross-validation error is at most the fraction of support vectors,
$\#\mathrm{SV}/n$.
:::

*In one line:* a model that depends on few training points cannot be very
wrong about the others — removing any of them does not even change it.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-svm-loo
Leave out a point $x_i$ that is not a support vector ($\alpha_i^* = 0$). The
remaining multipliers are still feasible for the dual without $x_i$ (the
equality $\sum\alpha_jy_j = 0$ is unaffected) and still satisfy all KKT
conditions of the reduced problem, which by convexity characterise its
optimum: the solution is unchanged. That solution classifies $x_i$
correctly, since $y_if(x_i) > 0$ for every point that is not a support vector
in the separable case ($y_if \ge 1$). Hence leave-one-out errors can only occur
at support vectors, and their number is at most $\#\mathrm{SV}$. (For the
soft margin, the same argument shows that a non-support vector with $y_if >
1$ is classified correctly when left out.) [@vapnik1998, ch. 10]
$\blacksquare$
:::

```{python}
from scipy.optimize import minimize
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut

r = np.random.default_rng(5)
Xq = np.vstack([r.normal([1, 1], 1.0, (25, 2)), r.normal([-1, -1], 1.0, (25, 2))]); yq = np.repeat([1, -1], 25)
Cq = 1.0
G = (yq[:, None] * yq[None, :]) * (Xq @ Xq.T)                       # y_i y_j x_i^T x_j
dual = minimize(lambda a: 0.5 * a @ G @ a - a.sum(), np.zeros(len(yq)), jac=lambda a: G @ a - 1,
                bounds=[(0, Cq)] * len(yq), constraints=[{"type": "eq", "fun": lambda a: a @ yq, "jac": lambda a: yq.astype(float)}],
                method="SLSQP", options={"ftol": 1e-12, "maxiter": 1000})
alpha = dual.x
w_dual = (alpha * yq) @ Xq                                            # @eq-svm-w
free = (alpha > 1e-6) & (alpha < Cq - 1e-6)
b_dual = np.mean(yq[free] - Xq[free] @ w_dual)
svc = SVC(kernel="linear", C=Cq).fit(Xq, yq)
print("dual by SLSQP: w =", w_dual.round(4), "b =", round(b_dual, 4), "| support vectors:", np.sum(alpha > 1e-6))
print("SVC:           w =", svc.coef_[0].round(4), "b =", svc.intercept_.round(4)[0], "| support vectors:", len(svc.support_))
dual_sk = np.zeros(len(yq)); dual_sk[svc.support_] = np.abs(svc.dual_coef_[0])        # dual_coef_ stores y_i alpha_i
print(f"max |alpha difference| = {np.abs(alpha - dual_sk).max():.1e}")
loo_err = 1 - cross_val_score(SVC(kernel="linear", C=Cq), Xq, yq, cv=LeaveOneOut()).mean()
print(f"leave-one-out error {loo_err:.3f}  <=  support-vector fraction {len(svc.support_) / len(yq):.3f}")
```

Our dual solution matches libsvm's multipliers (`dual_coef_` stores
$y_i\alpha_i$ for the support vectors), and the leave-one-out error is well
below the support-vector fraction. With overlapping classes many points are
inside the street, so the bound is loose; it is informative when the support
vectors are few.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla4-dual-easy}
## Easy — reading the multipliers
An SVM with $C = 2$ has, at the optimum, multipliers $\alpha = (0, 0.7, 2,
0, 2)$ for five training points. For each point, say whether it is outside
the street, on an edge, or inside the street / misclassified. Which points
determine $w$? Can you tell which of the points with $\alpha_i = C$ are
misclassified?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Use the three cases of complementary slackness in @thm-svm-dual.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Points 1 and 4 ($\alpha = 0$): on or outside the street — not support vectors
($\alpha_i = 0$ allows $y_if_i \ge 1$, including exactly on the edge, a
degenerate case). Point 2 ($0 < \alpha < C$): exactly on an edge, $y_if_2 =
1$. Points 3 and 5 ($\alpha = C$): $y_if_i \le 1$ — inside the street or on
the wrong side. $w = 0.7y_2x_2 + 2y_3x_3 + 2y_5x_5$. The multipliers alone do
not say whether points 3 and 5 are misclassified: that needs the score
$y_if_i$ (negative means misclassified). A common error is to call every
support vector "misclassified".
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-dual-medium}
## Medium — checking the KKT conditions
For `SVC(kernel="linear", C=1)` fitted on the 50 points of the dual example,
compute $y_if(x_i)$ for every point and check numerically each of the three
complementary-slackness statements of @thm-svm-dual, using `support_` and
`dual_coef_`. How many points are on the edges, how many inside the street,
how many misclassified?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`decision_function` gives $f(x_i)$. Rebuild the full vector of $\alpha$ with
zeros for non-support vectors. Use tolerances around $10^{-3}$: libsvm stops
at `tol=1e-3`.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
yf = yq * svc.decision_function(Xq)
a = dual_sk
tol = 1e-3
print("alpha = 0 but y f < 1 - tol:", np.sum((a < tol) & (yf < 1 - tol)))
print("0 < alpha < C but |y f - 1| > tol:", np.sum((a > tol) & (a < Cq - tol) & (np.abs(yf - 1) > tol)))
print("y f < 1 - tol but alpha < C - tol:", np.sum((yf < 1 - tol) & (a < Cq - tol)))
print(f"on an edge: {np.sum((a > tol) & (a < Cq - tol))}, inside the street but correct: {np.sum((yf > 0) & (yf < 1 - tol))}, "
      f"misclassified: {np.sum(yf < 0)}")
```
All three violation counts are zero (up to the solver's tolerance). The
support vectors split into the few free ones on the edges, which fix $b$, and
the bounded ones inside the street or on the wrong side. Reading these counts
is a quick diagnosis: very many bounded support vectors mean heavily
overlapping classes or a $C$ too small. The usual mistake is to forget that
`dual_coef_` contains $y_i\alpha_i$ (signed), not $\alpha_i$.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-dual-hard}
## Hard — how tight is the bound?
For the breast-cancer data (standardised), compute for `SVC(kernel="linear")`
with $C \in \{0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10\}$ the fraction of support vectors, the
leave-one-out error, and the 10-fold cross-validated error. When is the bound
of @thm-svm-loo useful, and which estimate would you report?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Put the scaler in a pipeline so that every leave-one-out fit rescales on its
own training data; 569 fits per value of $C$ are fast for a linear SVM.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
for Cc in (0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10):
    pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=Cc))
    sv_frac = len(pipe.fit(Xb, yb01)[-1].support_) / len(yb01)
    loo = 1 - cross_val_score(pipe, Xb, yb01, cv=LeaveOneOut()).mean()
    cv10 = 1 - cross_val_score(pipe, Xb, yb01, cv=StratifiedKFold(10, shuffle=True, random_state=0)).mean()
    print(f"C = {Cc:6}: support vectors {sv_frac:.3f} | LOO error {loo:.3f} | 10-fold error {cv10:.3f}")
```
For small $C$ most points are support vectors and the bound says almost
nothing; as $C$ grows the support vectors become few and the bound becomes
informative, but always remains above the leave-one-out error, which is the
estimate to report (with 10-fold CV as a cheaper alternative). The bound is
useful as a free sanity check — computed from one fit — and as a theoretical
explanation of why sparse solutions generalise. Mistake to avoid: fitting the
scaler once on all the data before leave-one-out.
:::

## Kernels {#sec-svm-kernels}

Many problems are not linearly separable in the original features, but become
so after a transformation: two classes separated by a circle become separable
by a plane after adding the feature $x_1^2 + x_2^2$ (@exr-mla2-choosing-medium).
In general we could map every point through a **feature map** $\varphi :
\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^D$ and fit a linear SVM to $\varphi(x_i)$. In the
dual @eq-svm-dual and in the prediction
$$
f(x) = w^\top\varphi(x) + b = \sum_i\alpha_iy_i\,\varphi(x_i)^\top\varphi(x) + b
$$ {#eq-svm-kernel-predict}
the map appears only through inner products. If a function
$K(x, z) = \varphi(x)^\top\varphi(z)$ can be computed directly, we never need
$\varphi$ — even when $D$ is enormous or infinite. This is the **kernel
trick**, introduced into machine learning by Aizerman, Braverman and Rozonoer
[@aizerman1964] and combined with the maximal margin by Boser, Guyon and
Vapnik [@boser1992].

| Kernel (scikit-learn `kernel=`) | $K(x, z)$ | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| `"linear"` | $x^\top z$ | — |
| `"poly"` | $(\gamma\,x^\top z + r)^p$ | `degree` $p$, `gamma` $\gamma$, `coef0` $r$ |
| `"rbf"` (Gaussian) | $\exp(-\gamma\lVert x - z\rVert^2)$ | `gamma` $\gamma > 0$ |
| `"sigmoid"` | $\tanh(\gamma\,x^\top z + r)$ | `gamma`, `coef0` |

: The kernels of `SVC`. The default `gamma="scale"` is $1/(d\cdot\operatorname{Var}(X))$, with the variance of all entries of the training matrix {#tbl-svm-kernels}

::: {#prp-svm-poly}
## The polynomial kernel is an inner product
For $x, z \in \mathbb{R}^d$, $(x^\top z + r)^2 = \varphi(x)^\top\varphi(z)$ with
$$
\varphi(x) = \big(x_1^2, \dots, x_d^2,\; \sqrt2x_jx_k\ (j < k),\; \sqrt{2r}\,x_1, \dots, \sqrt{2r}\,x_d,\; r\big),
$$
a vector of dimension $\binom{d+2}{2}$: all monomials of degree at most 2.
:::

*In one line:* squaring an inner product computes, in $O(d)$ operations, the
inner product of the $O(d^2)$ quadratic features.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-svm-poly
$(x^\top z + r)^2 = (\sum_jx_jz_j)^2 + 2r\sum_jx_jz_j + r^2 = \sum_jx_j^2z_j^2 +
2\sum_{j<k}x_jx_kz_jz_k + \sum_j2rx_jz_j + r^2$, which is $\varphi(x)^\top
\varphi(z)$ term by term. Counting coordinates: $d$ squares, $\binom d2$
products, $d$ linear terms and one constant, $\binom{d+2}{2}$ in total. For
degree $p$ the same expansion (multinomial theorem) gives all monomials of
degree $\le p$, $\binom{d+p}{p}$ of them [@scholkopf2002, §2.1]. $\blacksquare$
:::

Which functions $K$ are inner products in *some* feature space? A necessary
condition is easy to prove; it is also sufficient.

::: {#thm-svm-psd}
## Kernels and positive semidefinite Gram matrices
If $K(x, z) = \varphi(x)^\top\varphi(z)$, then for any points $x_1, \dots,
x_m$ the **Gram matrix** $G_{ij} = K(x_i, x_j)$ is symmetric positive
semidefinite. Conversely (Mercer; Moore–Aronszajn), every symmetric $K$ whose
Gram matrices are all positive semidefinite is an inner product
$\langle\varphi(x), \varphi(z)\rangle$ in some Hilbert space.
:::

*In one line:* a function is a valid kernel exactly when it never produces a
"negative squared length" — and then the dual remains a convex problem.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-svm-psd (first part) and remarks
Symmetry is clear. For any $c \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $c^\top Gc = \sum_{ij}c_ic_j
\varphi(x_i)^\top\varphi(x_j) = \lVert\sum_ic_i\varphi(x_i)\rVert^2 \ge 0$.
$\blacksquare$ The converse constructs $\varphi(x) = K(x, \cdot)$ in the space
of functions spanned by the $K(x, \cdot)$ with the inner product
$\langle K(x, \cdot), K(z, \cdot)\rangle = K(x, z)$ — the **reproducing
kernel Hilbert space** [@aronszajn1950; @scholkopf2002, §2.2]; Mercer's
theorem gives an explicit eigen-expansion for continuous kernels on compact
sets [@mercer1909]. Positive semidefiniteness is what makes the quadratic
form in @eq-svm-dual concave, so that the dual has no spurious local optima.
:::

::: {#prp-svm-rbf}
## The Gaussian kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map
For $x, z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\gamma > 0$,
$$
e^{-\gamma(x - z)^2} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty\varphi_k(x)\varphi_k(z),\qquad
\varphi_k(x) = e^{-\gamma x^2}\sqrt{\frac{(2\gamma)^k}{k!}}\,x^k .
$$
Hence the RBF kernel is a valid kernel, whose feature space contains
(weighted) monomials of every degree; the same holds in $d$ dimensions, where
$K$ factorises over coordinates.
:::

*In one line:* the Gaussian kernel is a polynomial kernel of infinite degree,
damped so that high degrees count less — which is why it can fit almost any
boundary.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-svm-rbf
$e^{-\gamma(x - z)^2} = e^{-\gamma x^2}e^{-\gamma z^2}e^{2\gamma xz}$ and
$e^{2\gamma xz} = \sum_k\frac{(2\gamma xz)^k}{k!}$ (the series converges for
all $x, z$); distributing $\sqrt{(2\gamma)^k/k!}$ and $e^{-\gamma(\cdot)^2}$ to
the two factors gives $\sum_k\varphi_k(x)\varphi_k(z)$. In $d$ dimensions
$e^{-\gamma\lVert x - z\rVert^2} = \prod_je^{-\gamma(x_j - z_j)^2}$, and a
product of kernels is a kernel (its feature map is the tensor product of the
feature maps). The sum of non-negative-definite rank-one terms gives
positive semidefinite Gram matrices, as in @thm-svm-psd. $\blacksquare$
:::

The **sigmoid** kernel, by contrast, is not positive semidefinite for all
parameters — its Gram matrices can have negative eigenvalues — so `SVC` with
`kernel="sigmoid"` solves a non-convex problem and can behave erratically; it
survives mainly for its resemblance to a neural network unit
[@scholkopf2002, §2.3]. The figure compares the four kernels on the same
non-linear problem.

```{python}
#| label: fig-svm-kernels
#| fig-cap: "The four kernels of SVC on 200 points of the two-moons problem (standardised; C = 1, default gamma; polynomial of degree 3 with coef0 = 1). The 5-fold cross-validated accuracy is in each title."
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
Xm, ym = make_moons(200, noise=0.25, random_state=0)
Xm = StandardScaler().fit_transform(Xm)
kernels = {"linear": SVC(kernel="linear"), "polynomial, degree 3": SVC(kernel="poly", degree=3, coef0=1),
           "Gaussian (RBF)": SVC(kernel="rbf"), "sigmoid": SVC(kernel="sigmoid")}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3.3), sharey=True)
for ax, (name, mdl) in zip(axes, kernels.items()):
    acc = cross_val_score(mdl, Xm, ym, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)).mean()
    mlalgbook.regions(ax, mdl.fit(Xm, ym), Xm, ym, s=10)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}\nCV accuracy {acc:.3f}", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The Gaussian kernel has two knobs. $\gamma$ sets the **reach** of each
training point: the kernel falls to $e^{-1}$ at distance $1/\sqrt\gamma$. A
small $\gamma$ gives smooth, almost linear boundaries; a large $\gamma$ makes
each support vector influence only its immediate surroundings, and the
boundary can wrap around individual points. $C$, as before, trades margin for
training errors. Explore the pair:

```{python}
#| echo: false
_Xm, _ym = make_moons(150, noise=0.3, random_state=3)
_Xm = StandardScaler().fit_transform(_Xm)
_gx = np.linspace(-2.6, 2.6, 52)
_xx, _yy = np.meshgrid(_gx, _gx)
_P = np.column_stack([_xx.ravel(), _yy.ravel()])
_Cs, _gs = [0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000], [0.05, 0.3, 1, 5, 30]
_rbf = []
for _C in _Cs:
    for _g in _gs:
        _m = SVC(kernel="rbf", C=_C, gamma=_g).fit(_Xm, _ym)
        _rbf.append({"C": _C, "gamma": _g, "pred": _m.predict(_P).astype(int).tolist(), "sv": int(len(_m.support_)),
                     "train": float(_m.score(_Xm, _ym)),
                     "cv": float(cross_val_score(SVC(kernel="rbf", C=_C, gamma=_g), _Xm, _ym, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)).mean())})
ojs_define(rbfPts=[{"x": float(a), "y": float(b), "label": int(c)} for (a, b), c in zip(_Xm, _ym)],
           rbfFits=_rbf, rbfGrid=_gx.tolist(), rbfCs=_Cs, rbfGammas=_gs)
```

### SVMs in practice

- **Scale the features** (inside a pipeline). Distances and inner products
  are computed in the units of the features: a feature measured in grams next
  to one on a 1–10 scale would dominate both the margin and the RBF kernel.
- **Tune $C$ and $\gamma$ together** on a logarithmic grid by
  cross-validation; their effects interact (a large $\gamma$ needs a smaller
  $C$ and vice versa) [@hsu2003].
- **More than two classes**: `SVC` trains one binary SVM for every pair of
  classes (one-vs-one, $K(K-1)/2$ models) and predicts by voting; `LinearSVC`
  uses one-vs-rest.
- **Probabilities**: SVM scores are not probabilities. `SVC(probability=True)`
  fits Platt's logistic map from scores to probabilities with an internal
  5-fold cross-validation [@platt2000], which is slower and can disagree with
  `predict` on borderline points.
- **Cost**: kernel SVMs need the $n \times n$ kernel matrix (or recompute it);
  training time grows between $n^2$ and $n^3$. Beyond a few tens of thousands
  of examples, prefer `LinearSVC` or `SGDClassifier(loss="hinge")`
  (@sec-opt-sgd), possibly on approximate kernel features.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla4-kernels-easy}
## Easy — a kernel value two ways
For $x = (1, 2)$ and $z = (3, -1)$, compute $(x^\top z + 1)^2$ directly and
through the explicit feature map of @prp-svm-poly; then compute the RBF
kernel with $\gamma = 0.5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$x^\top z = 1$. The feature map has 6 coordinates for $d = 2$: $x_1^2, x_2^2,
\sqrt2x_1x_2, \sqrt2x_1, \sqrt2x_2, 1$ (with $r = 1$).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$(1 + 1)^2 = 4$. With $\varphi(x) = (1, 4, 2\sqrt2, \sqrt2, 2\sqrt2, 1)$ and
$\varphi(z) = (9, 1, -3\sqrt2, 3\sqrt2, -\sqrt2, 1)$: $9 + 4 - 12 + 6 - 4 + 1
= 4$. RBF: $\lVert x - z\rVert^2 = 4 + 9 = 13$, $e^{-6.5} \approx 0.0015$.
```{python}
phi = lambda v: np.array([v[0]**2, v[1]**2, np.sqrt(2) * v[0] * v[1], np.sqrt(2) * v[0], np.sqrt(2) * v[1], 1.0])
x_, z_ = np.array([1.0, 2.0]), np.array([3.0, -1.0])
print((x_ @ z_ + 1) ** 2, phi(x_) @ phi(z_), np.exp(-0.5 * np.sum((x_ - z_) ** 2)))
```
The RBF value is tiny: the two points are far apart relative to the reach
$1/\sqrt{0.5} \approx 1.4$, so under this kernel they barely "see" each
other. Forgetting the $\sqrt2$ factors in the feature map is the classic slip.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-kernels-medium}
## Medium — positive semidefinite or not
For 100 random points in $\mathbb{R}^5$, compute the smallest eigenvalue of
the Gram matrices of the RBF kernel ($\gamma = 0.2$) and of the sigmoid kernel
$\tanh(\gamma x^\top z + r)$ for $(\gamma, r) = (0.2, 0)$ and $(0.2, -1)$.
Then verify that `SVC(kernel="precomputed")` given the RBF Gram matrix
reproduces `SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=0.2)`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`sklearn.metrics.pairwise` has `rbf_kernel` and `sigmoid_kernel`;
`np.linalg.eigvalsh` returns eigenvalues in ascending order. For the
precomputed SVM, prediction needs the kernel between the test and the
training points.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import rbf_kernel, sigmoid_kernel
Z5 = np.random.default_rng(6).normal(size=(100, 5)); lab5 = (Z5[:, 0] * Z5[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
print("RBF: smallest eigenvalue", f"{np.linalg.eigvalsh(rbf_kernel(Z5, gamma=0.2))[0]:.2e}")
for coef0 in (0, -1):
    print(f"sigmoid (gamma 0.2, coef0 {coef0}): smallest eigenvalue {np.linalg.eigvalsh(sigmoid_kernel(Z5, gamma=0.2, coef0=coef0))[0]:.3f}")
pre = SVC(kernel="precomputed").fit(rbf_kernel(Z5, gamma=0.2), lab5)
direct = SVC(kernel="rbf", gamma=0.2).fit(Z5, lab5)
Znew = np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=(20, 5))
print("same decisions:", np.allclose(pre.decision_function(rbf_kernel(Znew, Z5, gamma=0.2)), direct.decision_function(Znew)))
```
The RBF Gram matrix is positive (semi)definite, its smallest eigenvalue
non-negative up to rounding; the sigmoid ones have clearly negative
eigenvalues — they are not valid kernels for these points. The precomputed
route gives identical decisions: an SVM only ever sees kernel values. Typical
slip: passing the test–test kernel instead of the test–train kernel to
`predict`.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-kernels-hard}
## Hard — tuning an RBF SVM on measurements
On the wine data, tune $C$ and $\gamma$ of an RBF `SVC` in a pipeline with
`StandardScaler` by 5-fold `GridSearchCV` on a $7 \times 7$ logarithmic grid;
draw the heat map of the cross-validated accuracy; estimate the accuracy of
the whole procedure by nested cross-validation; and compare with the linear
SVM of @exr-mla4-soft-hard. Then remove the scaler and repeat the grid search:
what happens, and why?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`GridSearchCV.cv_results_["mean_test_score"]` reshaped to the grid gives the
heat map. Without scaling, look at the ranges of the wine features (proline is
in the hundreds or thousands, most others below 10).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
#| label: fig-svm-wine-grid
#| fig-cap: "Cross-validated accuracy of an RBF SVM on the standardised wine data over a grid of C and γ. The good region is a diagonal band: larger γ needs smaller C."
C_grid, g_grid = np.logspace(-2, 4, 7), np.logspace(-4, 2, 7)
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf"))
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {"svc__C": C_grid, "svc__gamma": g_grid}, cv=inner).fit(Xw, yw)
acc_grid = gs.cv_results_["mean_test_score"].reshape(len(C_grid), len(g_grid))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.2, 4))
im = ax.imshow(acc_grid, origin="lower", cmap="Blues", vmin=0.3, vmax=1)
ax.set_xticks(range(7), [f"{g:g}" for g in g_grid], rotation=45); ax.set_yticks(range(7), [f"{c:g}" for c in C_grid])
ax.set_xlabel("γ"); ax.set_ylabel("C"); ax.grid(False); fig.colorbar(im, label="CV accuracy"); plt.show()
nested_rbf = cross_val_score(GridSearchCV(pipe, {"svc__C": C_grid, "svc__gamma": g_grid}, cv=inner), Xw, yw, cv=outer)
raw = GridSearchCV(SVC(kernel="rbf"), {"C": C_grid, "gamma": g_grid}, cv=inner).fit(Xw, yw)
print(f"best (scaled): {gs.best_params_}, CV accuracy {gs.best_score_:.3f}; nested estimate {nested_rbf.mean():.3f} ± {nested_rbf.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(5):.3f}")
print(f"without scaling: best {raw.best_params_}, CV accuracy {raw.best_score_:.3f}")
```
With scaling, a broad diagonal band of $(C, \gamma)$ reaches very high
accuracy, comparable with the linear SVM (the wine classes are nearly linearly
separable, so the kernel adds little here). Without scaling, distances are
dominated by proline and magnesium, the kernel effectively sees one or two
features, and even the best grid point is much worse. For the project the
lesson is direct: the fruit measurements are on very different scales
(grams, millimetres, 1–10 scores), and any distance- or kernel-based model
must be preceded by scaling fitted inside the cross-validation. Mistakes to
avoid: a grid that is too narrow (check that the best point is not on its
edge) and reporting `best_score_` instead of the nested estimate.
:::

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** An SVM with an RBF kernel is a strong competitor for a
small table of continuous measurements with a handful of classes: it is the
natural model to compare with $k$-NN, because both rely on **distances**
between fruits — and both therefore require **scaling** inside a pipeline.
For five classes `SVC` trains ten one-vs-one classifiers; its errors can be
read from the same per-class confusion matrix. Two cautions: tune $C$ and
$\gamma$ together, and report a nested estimate when the comparison between
models is the result.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **No scaling.** The margin and the kernels are geometric: features with
  large ranges dominate.
- **Reading $C$ as a penalty strength.** It is the *inverse*: large $C$ means
  little regularisation.
- **Tuning $C$ and $\gamma$ separately**, or on a grid whose optimum sits on
  the border.
- **Using decision scores as probabilities**, or trusting
  `probability=True` outputs without checking their calibration.
- **Deleting outliers to improve the fit.** Lower $C$, or justify the removal
  by what the point is, not by its effect on the score.
- **Kernel SVMs on large data sets**: quadratic memory and super-quadratic
  time; use linear models or approximations.
- **The sigmoid kernel** is not a valid kernel for many parameter values.
:::

## Summary

- The signed distance from $w^\top x + b = 0$ is $(w^\top x + b)/\lVert
  w\rVert$; the maximal margin classifier minimises $\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2$
  subject to $y_if(x_i) \ge 1$ — a convex problem with a unique solution.
- The soft margin adds slacks at price $C$; it is equivalent to minimising the
  hinge loss plus $\frac{1}{2C}\lVert w\rVert^2$. The hinge bounds the 0–1 loss
  and is zero for points beyond the margin.
- The dual depends on the data only through inner products; $w = \sum_i
  \alpha_iy_ix_i$, with $\alpha_i > 0$ only for support vectors (KKT), and
  the leave-one-out error is at most the fraction of support vectors.
- Kernels replace inner products by $K(x, z)$; valid kernels have positive
  semidefinite Gram matrices. The RBF kernel's feature space is
  infinite-dimensional; $\gamma$ sets the reach, $C$ the trade-off.
- In practice: scale, tune $C$ and $\gamma$ jointly by cross-validation, use
  linear SVMs for large data.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-mla4-representer}
**The representer property.** Show that for any $w \in \mathbb{R}^D$ the
objective @eq-svm-hinge (with $\varphi(x_i)$ in place of $x_i$) does not
increase when $w$ is replaced by its projection onto the span of the
$\varphi(x_i)$. Conclude that an optimal $w$ is a combination of the training
points even without going through the dual.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
Write $w = w_\parallel + w_\perp$, with $w_\parallel$ in the span $S$ of the
$\varphi(x_i)$ and $w_\perp$ orthogonal to $S$. Then $w^\top\varphi(x_i) =
w_\parallel^\top\varphi(x_i)$ for every $i$, so the hinge terms are
unchanged, while $\lVert w\rVert^2 = \lVert w_\parallel\rVert^2 + \lVert
w_\perp\rVert^2 \ge \lVert w_\parallel\rVert^2$. Hence the projection is never
worse, and any minimiser has $w_\perp = 0$: $w = \sum_i\beta_i\varphi(x_i)$.
This is the **representer theorem** in its simplest form; it holds for every
loss that depends on $w$ only through the values $w^\top\varphi(x_i)$, plus an
increasing function of $\lVert w\rVert$ [@scholkopf2001]. It is why kernel
ridge regression and kernel logistic regression also work with kernels.
:::

::: {#exr-mla4-svm-vs-logistic}
**Hinge versus logistic.** On the moons data of @fig-svm-kernels, compare a
linear SVM and logistic regression on the *same* polynomial features of
degree 3 (pipeline with scaling), each with its regularisation chosen by
cross-validation. Are their boundaries and accuracies different? What remains
specific to the SVM?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
```{python}
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
cv5 = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
svm_poly = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(3), StandardScaler(), LinearSVC(max_iter=50_000)),
                        {"linearsvc__C": np.logspace(-3, 2, 11)}, cv=cv5)
log_poly = GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(PolynomialFeatures(3), StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000)),
                        {"logisticregression__C": np.logspace(-3, 3, 13)}, cv=cv5)
for name, m_ in (("linear SVM", svm_poly), ("logistic", log_poly)):
    print(f"{name:10s}: nested CV accuracy {cross_val_score(m_, Xm, ym, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)).mean():.3f}")
```
On the same features the two linear models perform almost identically: the
choice of features and of the regularisation matters far more than hinge
versus logistic loss [@hastie2009, §12.3.2]. What remains specific to the SVM
is sparsity in the dual (support vectors) and, with kernels, the ability to
work in feature spaces that are never built; what remains specific to
logistic regression is calibrated probabilities.
:::

  kernels.

  @vapnik1998 — the theory behind them.
- @scholkopf2002, ch. 1–2 and 7 — kernels, feature spaces, the representer
  theorem and SVMs in depth.

  @thm-svm-dual.
